# Introduction to R

First, lets install some packages we will use today: 

## Installing packages

```{r, eval=FALSE}

install.packages("data.table")
install.packages("ggplot2")
install.packages("forcats")
install.packages("reshape2")

```

If you are questioned if you want to install the packages from source or update other packages, you can accept. If you face problems, try again answering `no`. 

### The libPaths problem: 

Optional, if the package installation doesn't work: If you get error messages that describe that you can't install the packages, the problem is likely that R has no writing access in the directory of your package library. 

```{r}
.libPaths() # This shows you the currently used directory (the first entry):
```

To solve the problem, we generate and use another directory for our libraries: 

```{r, eval = FALSE}
user_lib <- Sys.getenv("R_LIBS_USER") # find personal standard library directory
dir.create(user_lib, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE) # Create directory
.libPaths(c(user_lib, .libPaths())) # Activate it
.libPaths() # check if it worked
```

The `.libPaths()` call should show the new directory as first entry. Restart `RStudio` and try to install the package again, using the `install.packages()` line above. 


Load packages: 

```{r}
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)

```




## Import data:

Lets explore our DepMap cell line model/patient data. First, we import it using `fread()` and assign it to the variable `models`: 

```{r, eval = FALSE}
models <- fread("input_data/Model.csv")
```

Importing and cleaning data can be complicated, and I want to make sure that everybody is working with the same data. Please execute this script, which loads packages and required input data. You can always re-load the script if you accidently replaced it.  

```{r}
source("R/prepare_everything.R")
```

```{r}
str(models)
```

`data.table` is a modern R package which introduces a compact syntax and very fast data handling. This is perfect for operations on the datasets we want to work with today. 
Data tables are enhanced `data.frames`, so if you are familiar with `data.frames` and `tidyverse` functions, you can use them here as well. 
Datatables/dataframes are perfect for storing different datatypes for many observations, e.g. age (numeric), sex (categorical), treatment status (logical), etc., across patients. Datatables are in most cases two-dimensional, with observations / measurements / patients in rows and features in columns. 

```{r}
head(models)
```

### Handling Datatables

The data table syntax consists of three elements: 

`DT[<rows>, <columns>, <by>]`. 

`<rows>` defines the rows to extract from the `DT`. Often used with filter criteria. 
`<columns>` defines the columns to select. Can also be used to create new columns or to execute functions in the data table. 
`by` defines variables to group the data by. Can be used to elegantly summarize the information of the datatable. 

Examples: 

To only select certain columns, we wrap them in `.()`.  This is usually done **after** the first comma: 

```{r}
models[, .(Sex, Age)]
```



Important operator: `.N` returns the number of rows.  

```{r}
models[, .N]
```

`.N` is expecially useful when combined with a grouping variable after the second comma. We can write `by = `, but we don't have to. 
Lets explore how many male and female patients (and patients with unknown sex) are in the dataset: 

```{r}
models[, .N, by = Sex]
```

This gives you a good overview on the options to subset the patients by. 

Get an overview over the number of entries for each cancer type (`OncotreeLineage`):

```{r}
models[, .N, by = OncotreeLineage]
```

### Filtering datatables

Filtering means creating a logical vector and only returning the rows where the vector is `TRUE`. 

| Operator | Description |
|---|---|
| `==` | is equal |
| `!=` | is unequal |
| `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=` | larger, smaller, greater or equal, ... |
| `%in%` | required if we filter for more than one entry |



Filtering criteria can be used and combined to subset the data. This returns entries for non-caucasian patients with breast or Lung cancer: 

```{r}
models[PatientRace != "caucasian" & 
    OncotreeLineage %in% c("Breast", "Lung")]
```

Lets combine filtering and column subsetting. This returns only the columns Sex and Age for female patients: 
```{r}
models[Sex == "Female", .(Sex, Age)]
```

How many entries for `female` patients older than `30` years are in `models`?

```{r}
models[Age > 30 & Sex == "Female", .N]
```

If we want to summarize rows like this, we can use summarizing functions instead of only counting rows. `mean()` returns the mean value of a vector: 

```{r}
models[, .(Age = mean(Age, na.rm = TRUE))]
```

Now, lets explore the mean age for each gender in the dataset: 

```{r}
models[, .(Age = mean(Age, na.rm = TRUE)), by = Sex]
```

Now its your turn: For patients with `breast` cancer, what is the number of observations and the mean age, for each gender? 

```{r}
models[OncotreeLineage == "Breast", .(n_patients = .N, Age = mean(Age, na.rm = TRUE)), by = Sex]
```

# NAs

`NAs` are missing values. They will occur in your data. Operations involving `NAs` often return `NA`. Therefore, many functions allow to ignore them: 

```{r}
sum(c(2, 12, NA))

sum(c(2, 12, NA), na.rm = TRUE)
```


`is.na()` tells us if a value is NA. This is useful for filtering entries. 

```{r}
models[is.na(Sex)]
```

We can create new columns with `by`, too: 

```{r}
models[, .(mean_age = mean(Age), N = .N), by = .(Age_is_NA = is.na(Age))]
```


# Coding exercise 2: Arrays

Arrays are great for storing large amounts of only-numeric data. In contrast to data.tables, they can have many more than two dimensions. One way of using these could be: 

1. dimension: Genes
2. dimension: drug treatments
3. dimension: technical replicates
4. media conditions
... 

Lets explore our expression dataset. How many dimensions does the object have? What do they store?

```{r}
str(expression)
```

We can subset arrays using vectors of numbers or characters: 

```{r}
str(expression[1:5,10:20])
str(expression[,c("STPG1", "CFTR")])
```

Other useful R functions: 

| Function | Returns / Explanation |
|---|---|
| `?mean()` | help and additional information on the `mean` function |
| `str()` | dataset structure |
| `dim()` | dimensions |
| `dimnames()` | dimension names |
| `intersect(a, b)` | elements in a and b |
| `setdiff()` | elements of a that are not in b |
| `cor()` | computes a correlation |












[order(-N)]



## For-loops

If you want to execute the same operation on many elements, you can use a loop: 

```{r}

for (gene in oncogenes) {
    print(paste0("Mean expression of ", gene, ": ", mean(expression[,gene], na.rm = TRUE)))
}

```

There are more options to do this. 

A very useful function to know is `apply()`. It allows very fast computations of aggregation functions (like `mean`, `sum` or `length`) on the whole array. Lets compute the mean expression for three genes across all columns of the dataset: 

```{r}
apply(expression[,oncogenes], 2, mean)
```
